texts.0: SP, due to an incomplete cross-check between the outside references and the altimeter while maneuvering in the pattern, did not hold the pattern altitude published in the LAP. Altitude deviated by more than 300 feet on the downwind and the divergence continued through the base turn. The IP had to intervene on the controls to re-establish the aircraft at pattern altitude.
texts.1: SP, due to a cross-check that stopped at the outside references during the pattern turns, did not maintain the published pattern altitude. Peak deviations reached 300 feet, at the limit of the standard, mainly as a descent inside the turns. SP started the correction only after repeated verbal prompting from the IP and the level-off was late.
texts.2: SP, due to pitch corrections applied without a matching power adjustment during the pattern turns, allowed altitude to depart from the published pattern altitude by 200 to 250 feet, outside the desired band but inside the maximum. SP identified the trend on the altimeter without prompting and re-established pattern altitude before the following turn. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP held the pattern altitude published in the LAP with a steady altimeter cross-check throughout the circuit. Deviations stayed within 150 feet and were corrected as they appeared, with small and coordinated pitch and power inputs. Bank and configuration changes did not disturb the altitude, and no prompting was needed at any point of the pattern.
texts.4: SP flew the entire pattern with the altimeter essentially fixed on the published pattern altitude. Deviations were of the order of 30 to 50 feet and were removed as they developed. Turns and configuration changes produced no measurable altitude excursion, and the level flight segments were held without visible correction.
texts.marginal: SP kept the pattern altitude within standards, but the deviations clustered in the upper part of the acceptable band, as a slow climb during the crosswind and base turns. Each correction was made, yet it followed the deviation instead of preventing it, and the altimeter was referenced only after the roll-out. SP is expected to anticipate the pitch and power required in the turns so that the altitude trend is contained rather than corrected.

texts_at.0: SP flew the pattern with the IP calling the altimeter back into the cross-check the instant each turn was complete, since holding pattern altitude through repeated turns and configuration changes has not yet been practiced without that call. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to return to the altimeter cross-check independently after each turn.
texts_at.1: SP held the pattern altitude published in the LAP to within approximately 300 feet, at the outer edge of the standard, due to the altimeter cross-check settling on the outside references for a beat longer than the technique calls for after each turn. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to return to the altimeter cross-check the instant each turn is complete rather than a beat after it.
texts_at.2: SP held pattern altitude within about 220 feet, due to a pitch correction applied without the matching power adjustment following in the same instant. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to bring the power adjustment into the same instant as the pitch correction rather than after it.
texts_at.3: SP held the pattern altitude within approximately 150 feet, due to the altimeter cross-check through the turns running a fraction behind the bank and configuration changes rather than matching them. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to keep the altimeter cross-check moving with the bank and configuration changes rather than trailing them.

texts_above.1: SP held the pattern altitude published in the LAP to within approximately 280 feet after the altimeter cross-check was called back in. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP held the pattern altitude published in the LAP within about 200 feet on every circuit, with small and coordinated pitch and power inputs correcting any deviation as it appeared. Anticipating the pitch and power required in the turns a moment earlier would tighten that figure further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good altitude discipline.
texts_above.3: SP held the pattern altitude within roughly 60 feet through every turn and configuration change, with no prompting needed at any point of the pattern. The only refinement available was to anticipate the pitch and power requirement a fraction earlier still on the tightest turns. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good altitude discipline.
texts_above.4: SP flew the entire pattern with the altimeter essentially fixed on the published pattern altitude, with turns and configuration changes producing no measurable excursion. The technique is already sound; nothing in the altitude cross-check needs to change. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent altitude discipline.

texts.3: SP flew each leg of the pattern at the airspeed published in the LAP, with deviations contained within 10 knots. Power was set together with each configuration change, so the speed stabilized quickly on every leg. Speed control required no prompting at any point of the pattern.
texts.4: SP held the published pattern airspeeds within a few knots on every leg, arriving on final exactly at the target speed. Each configuration change was anticipated with the corresponding power setting, so no speed excursion developed. Speed control was precise and continuous throughout the circuit.

texts_at.1: SP held the pattern airspeeds published in the LAP to within approximately 20 knots, at the outer edge of the standard, due to the power reduction being made just after the flap and gear extension rather than with it. texts_at.2: SP held pattern airspeed within about 15 knots, due to a power setting applied a beat after the configuration change rather than together with it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to set the power in the same instant as the configuration change.
texts_at.3: SP held pattern airspeed within approximately 10 knots, due to the power setting for each leg being refined a fraction after the configuration change rather than sized correctly the first time. texts_above.1: SP held the pattern airspeeds published in the LAP to within approximately 18 knots after the power setting was called together with the configuration change. texts_above.2: SP flew each leg of the pattern at the airspeed published in the LAP within about 15 knots, with power set together with each configuration change so the speed stabilized quickly on every leg. Anticipating the configuration change a fraction earlier would tighten that figure further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound speed management.
texts_above.3: SP held the published pattern airspeeds within a few knots on every leg, anticipating each configuration change with the corresponding power setting so no speed excursion developed. The only refinement available was to anticipate the power setting a fraction earlier still on the busiest legs. texts.0: SP, due to turns flown without an established lead point or roll-out reference, did not exit the pattern turns on the headings that define the downwind and base legs. Roll-out headings were more than 10 degrees off, so the legs were flown on the wrong track and the pattern geometry was lost. The IP had to intervene to re-establish the aircraft on the correct leg.
texts.1: SP, due to a roll-out started at the target heading rather than before it, did not exit the pattern turns on the required headings. Errors of about 10 degrees were reached, at the limit of the standard. SP corrected only after the IP called the heading, after a large part of the leg had already been flown displaced.
texts.2: SP, due to a variable rate of roll in the pattern turns, exited them 6 to 9 degrees off the required headings, outside the desired band but within the maximum. SP detected the error on the HSI and corrected it within a few seconds, before the leg was affected. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP exited every pattern turn within 5 degrees of the required heading, using a consistent lead point for each roll-out. The downwind and base legs were established on the correct headings from the moment the wings were level. No corrective heading changes were needed after the roll-outs.
texts.4: SP rolled out of every pattern turn essentially on the required heading, with errors of one to two degrees. The lead point and the rate of roll were matched to the angle of bank on each turn, so no heading correction followed any roll-out. The legs of the pattern were established immediately and held.
texts.marginal: SP exited the pattern turns within standards, but consistently a few degrees short of the required heading in the same direction, and each roll-out was followed by a small corrective turn. The headings were achieved, yet the technique relied on that second correction. SP is expected to adjust the lead point so that the required heading is reached on the initial roll-out.

texts_at.0: SP flew the pattern turns with the IP calling the lead point before the target heading was reached, since judging that lead from the rate of roll has not yet been practiced without that call. texts_at.1: SP exited the pattern turns within approximately 10 degrees of the required headings, at the outer edge of the standard, due to the roll-out being started at the target heading rather than led into it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to begin the roll-out before the target heading is reached rather than at the moment it is reached.
texts_at.2: SP exited the pattern turns within about 7 degrees of the required headings, due to the lead point being judged a beat late relative to the rate of roll used. texts_at.3: SP exited every pattern turn within approximately 5 degrees of the required heading, due to the lead point being set correctly but the roll-out itself finishing a fraction after the wings reached the target bank. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to finish the roll-out in the same motion as the wings reach the target bank.

texts_above.1: SP exited the pattern turns within approximately 9 degrees of the required headings after the lead point was called. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP exited every pattern turn within about 7 degrees of the required heading, using a consistent lead point so the downwind and base legs were established on the correct headings from the moment the wings were level. Setting the lead point a fraction earlier on the tightest turns would tighten that figure further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid heading capture.
texts_above.3: SP exited every pattern turn within a couple of degrees of the required heading with no corrective heading changes needed after any roll-out, the lead point matched to the angle of bank on each turn. The only refinement available was to match the lead point to the bank a fraction more finely still. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate heading capture.
texts_above.4: SP rolled out of every pattern turn essentially on the required heading, with the lead point and the rate of roll matched to the angle of bank on each turn so the legs of the pattern were established immediately and held. The technique is already sound; nothing in the lead-point judgement needs to change. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary heading capture.

error_modes.label: Ground track over the LAP pattern points

texts.0: SP, due to weak identification and use of the ground references that define the pattern, did not overfly the points of the traffic pattern described in the LAP. The aircraft passed well beyond the 0.5 NM maximum radius, the downwind was flown wide and the published pattern geometry was no longer recognizable. The IP had to direct the corrections needed to re-establish the pattern.
texts.1: SP, due to a ground reference acquired late after each turn, did not track over the pattern points as described in the LAP. The aircraft passed at about 0.5 NM from them, at the limit of the permitted radius. SP corrected the displacement only after the IP pointed it out, and the correction was applied after the point had been passed.
texts.2: SP, due to a drift correction that was set but not refined, overflew the pattern points at 0.3 to 0.4 NM from them, inside the 0.5 NM maximum but wider than intended. SP recognized the displacement against the ground references and adjusted the track before the following point, without IP prompting.
texts.3: SP overflew each point of the traffic pattern described in the LAP well inside the 0.5 NM maximum radius. The ground references were identified early and the drift correction was set on each leg, so the track matched the published pattern. No prompting or correction from the IP was required.
texts.4: SP tracked essentially over the pattern points described in the LAP on every leg, with displacements of a small fraction of the permitted radius. Drift was assessed and corrected before it displaced the track, and the pattern flown reproduced the published geometry. The ground references were used continuously and without hesitation.
texts.marginal: SP overflew the pattern points inside the 0.5 NM radius, but consistently on the wide side and with the displacement growing from downwind to base. The standard was met, yet the margin available for a correction was small. SP is expected to set the drift correction earlier on each leg so that the track stays close to the published points rather than close to the limit.

texts_at.0: SP flew over the pattern points with the IP calling the ground reference to acquire during each turn, since identifying the reference during the turn itself, rather than after rolling out, has not yet been practiced without that call. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to identify the ground reference independently during the next turn.
texts_at.1: SP overflew the points of the traffic pattern described in the LAP at approximately 0.45 NM from them, at the outer edge of the permitted radius, due to the ground reference being acquired only after the turn onto the leg rather than during it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to identify the ground reference during the turn itself rather than after rolling out of it.
texts_at.2: SP overflew the pattern points within the 0.5 NM maximum radius, due to the drift correction being set once at the start of the leg rather than refined as it progressed. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to refine the drift correction through the leg rather than setting it once at the start.
texts_at.3: SP overflew each point of the traffic pattern described in the LAP well inside the 0.5 NM maximum radius, due to the drift correction being confirmed a fraction after roll-out rather than as part of it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to confirm the drift correction as part of the roll-out itself.

texts_above.1: SP overflew the points of the traffic pattern described in the LAP, tracking well inside the 0.5 NM maximum radius after the ground reference was called during the turn. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP overflew every point of the traffic pattern described in the LAP with the ground references identified early and the drift correction set on each leg, tracking a comfortable margin inside the 0.5 NM maximum radius. Identifying the reference a moment earlier still would widen that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady track discipline.
texts_above.3: SP tracked essentially over the pattern points described in the LAP on every leg, with drift assessed and corrected before it could displace the track and the ground references used continuously. The only refinement available was to assess the drift a fraction sooner still on the fastest legs. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good track discipline.
texts_above.4: SP tracked essentially over the pattern points described in the LAP on every leg, with displacements of a small fraction of the permitted radius and the pattern flown reproducing the published geometry exactly. The technique is already sound; nothing in the drift assessment needs to change. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior track discipline.

error_modes.label: Spacing to other traffic and clearing

texts.0: SP, due to loss of situational awareness of the aircraft's position in the pattern relative to the preceding traffic, did not maintain proper spacing and did not clear constantly. Spacing closed to the point where the published sequence could no longer be flown, and the preceding aircraft was never acquired visually. The IP had to take corrective action to restore separation in the pattern.
texts.1: SP, due to degraded situational awareness of the sequence in the pattern, did not maintain proper spacing to the other traffic and cleared only intermittently. Spacing reduced to the minimum that still allowed the pattern to be flown. SP extended the leg to open the spacing only after the IP called the traffic.
texts.2: SP, due to situational awareness that stayed focused on the aircraft immediately ahead, allowed the spacing to become tighter than planned on the downwind. SP acquired the traffic during the clearing scan and adjusted the leg length in time to restore proper spacing. No IP prompting or intervention was required.
texts.3: SP maintained proper spacing to the other traffic in the pattern and cleared constantly on every leg. The sequence was tracked from the position reports and confirmed visually, and the leg lengths were adjusted to keep the spacing stable. No prompting was required at any point.
texts.4: SP maintained proper spacing to all other traffic throughout the pattern, adjusting the legs early and by small amounts so the sequence was never in doubt. The clearing scan was continuous and each aircraft in the pattern was acquired visually before it became a factor. The pattern was flown with the traffic picture fully maintained.
texts.marginal: SP maintained the required spacing and cleared, but the lookout scan concentrated on the aircraft immediately ahead and the spacing adjustments were made late in the leg. Separation was never in question, yet the picture of the rest of the pattern was thin. SP is expected to broaden the clearing scan to the whole pattern and to adjust spacing earlier, so it is managed rather than recovered.

texts_at.0: SP maintained spacing in the pattern with the IP calling the traffic that was clear of the immediate leg, since broadening the clearing scan to the whole pattern has not yet been practiced without that call. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to broaden the clearing scan independently on the next pattern.
texts_at.1: SP maintained proper spacing to the other traffic in the pattern, due to the clearing scan concentrating on the aircraft immediately ahead for longer than the technique calls for before widening to the rest of the pattern. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to widen the clearing scan to the rest of the pattern sooner rather than concentrating on the aircraft immediately ahead.
texts_at.2: SP maintained proper spacing and cleared through the pattern, due to a spacing adjustment being made a beat after the closure was noticed rather than as it was noticed. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to act on the closure the instant it is noticed rather than a moment later.
texts_at.3: SP maintained proper spacing to the other traffic and cleared constantly, due to the leg length being adjusted a fraction after the spacing trend was visible rather than as it appeared. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to adjust the leg length as the spacing trend first appears.

texts_above.1: SP maintained proper spacing to the other traffic in the pattern, adjusting the leg after the wider traffic picture was called out rather than needing it repeated. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP maintained proper spacing to the other traffic in the pattern on every leg, tracking the sequence from the position reports and confirming it visually with the leg lengths adjusted to keep the spacing stable. Broadening the clearing scan a fraction sooner would widen that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable spacing judgement.
texts_above.3: SP maintained proper spacing throughout the pattern, adjusting the legs early and by small amounts so the sequence was never in doubt and each aircraft was acquired visually before it became a factor. The only refinement available was to acquire the traffic a fraction sooner still on the busiest circuits. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise spacing judgement.
texts_above.4: SP maintained proper spacing to all other traffic throughout the pattern, with the clearing scan continuous and the pattern flown with the traffic picture fully maintained at every point. The technique is already sound; nothing in the clearing scan needs to change. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate spacing judgement.

texts.0: SP, due to non-standard phraseology that left the intention ambiguous to the controller, did not give the standardized position reports of the traffic pattern. Reports were omitted at prescribed points and those transmitted had to be queried by ATC. The IP had to make the calls for the pattern to continue as cleared.
texts.1: SP, due to phraseology built during the transmission instead of prepared before it, did not give the standardized position reports as required. More than one report was transmitted with non-standard wording and away from the prescribed point. SP used the correct format only after the IP dictated the call.
texts.2: SP, due to a report initiated before the wording was ready, departed from the standard phraseology on one call and transmitted another report late relative to the prescribed point. All required reports were made and SP corrected the format on the following call without prompting. No IP intervention was needed.
texts.3: SP gave all the standardized position reports at the prescribed points of the pattern, with correct phraseology and content. The calls were made with the aircraft stabilized on each leg and did not interfere with the flying task. No prompting or correction was required.
texts.4: SP gave every standardized position report at the correct point, with concise and fully standard phraseology. The calls were timed so they neither blocked other stations nor competed with a control input. Read-backs of ATC instructions were complete and accurate throughout the pattern.
texts.marginal: SP gave all the required position reports with acceptable phraseology, but several calls were rushed and made while the aircraft was still in the turn. The content was correct, yet the delivery was compressed and twice overlapped another station. SP is expected to prepare the call before keying and to transmit it with the aircraft stabilized on the leg.

texts_at.0: SP made the position reports with the IP calling the standard phraseology before the transmitter was keyed, since preparing the wording before transmitting has not yet been practiced without that call. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to prepare the wording independently before the next call.
texts_at.1: SP gave the standardized position reports of the traffic pattern, due to the phrasing for one call being built during the transmission rather than prepared before it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to prepare the phrasing of each call before keying the transmitter rather than while transmitting.
texts_at.2: SP gave the required position reports with standard phraseology, due to a report being initiated a beat before the wording was fully ready rather than once it was complete. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to complete the wording before keying the transmitter rather than starting to transmit while still composing it.
texts_at.3: SP gave all the standardized position reports at the prescribed points with correct phraseology, due to one call being made a fraction before the aircraft had fully stabilized on the leg rather than once it had. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to wait for the aircraft to stabilize on the leg before making the call.

texts_above.1: SP gave the standardized position reports of the traffic pattern, completing one call in standard phraseology after the wording was called prepared rather than needing it dictated. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP gave all the standardized position reports at the prescribed points of the pattern, with correct phraseology and content and the calls made with the aircraft stabilized on each leg. Preparing the wording a moment earlier still would make the delivery even more fluent. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured radio technique.
texts_above.3: SP gave every standardized position report with concise, correct phraseology and content, timing the calls so they neither blocked other stations nor competed with a control input. The only refinement available was to prepare the next call during the previous quiet interval rather than as the point is reached. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good radio technique.
texts_above.4: SP gave every standardized position report at the correct point with concise and fully standard phraseology, with read-backs of ATC instructions complete and accurate throughout the pattern. The technique is already sound; nothing in the call timing needs to change. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior radio technique.

error_modes.label: Radio monitoring and correlation of other traffic

texts.0: SP, due to an attention bottleneck on the flying task that left the radio unmonitored, did not check the position of other aircraft against their position reports and the ATC instructions. Calls addressed to the aircraft were missed and an ATC instruction was not complied with. The IP had to answer for the aircraft and restore compliance with the clearance.
texts.1: SP, due to attention captured by the flying task at the expense of the radio, did not build the traffic picture from the position reports of the other aircraft. Two transmissions addressed to the aircraft went unanswered and the ATC instruction was applied late. SP acted only after the IP repeated the instruction in the cockpit.
texts.2: SP, due to attention held on a single leg of the pattern, missed one position report from another aircraft and did not initially place that traffic in the sequence. SP asked for and obtained the information on the next transmission and corrected the traffic picture before it became a factor. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP monitored the radio throughout the pattern and checked the position of the other aircraft against their position reports and the ATC instructions. Every call addressed to the aircraft was answered promptly and correctly read back. The traffic picture was maintained without prompting for the whole circuit.
texts.4: SP monitored the radio continuously and maintained an accurate picture of every aircraft in the pattern from their reports and the ATC instructions. Clearances were read back completely and complied with without delay, including one change of sequence. Radio work was integrated with the flying task with no degradation of either.
texts.marginal: SP monitored the radio and complied with the ATC instructions, but the correlation of other traffic to their position reports was made only when that traffic became relevant to his own leg. Nothing was missed, yet the picture was reconstructed on demand rather than kept current. SP is expected to track all pattern traffic continuously so the sequence is known before it has to be used.

texts_at.0: SP monitored the radio with the IP calling attention back to a transmission addressed to the aircraft, since keeping the radio in a continuous scan alongside the flying task has not yet been practiced without that call. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to keep the radio in that scan independently on the next pattern.
texts_at.1: SP monitored the radio and checked the position of other aircraft against their position reports and the ATC instructions, due to one call addressed to the aircraft being answered only after a brief pause on the flying task rather than promptly. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to keep the radio in the scan continuously rather than pausing on the flying task before answering.
texts_at.2: SP monitored the radio and built the traffic picture from the position reports, due to attention being held on a single leg of the pattern for longer than the technique calls for before returning to the wider picture. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to return to the wider traffic picture sooner rather than holding attention on a single leg.
texts_at.3: SP monitored the radio throughout the pattern and checked the position of other aircraft against their reports, due to the correlation of one aircraft's position being made a fraction after it was first heard rather than as it was heard. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to correlate each position report as it is heard rather than shortly after.

texts_above.1: SP monitored the radio and checked the position of other aircraft against their position reports, answering one call after attention was called back to it. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP monitored the radio throughout the pattern and checked the position of the other aircraft against their position reports and the ATC instructions, with every call addressed to the aircraft answered promptly and correctly read back. Correlating each report a moment sooner would sharpen the traffic picture further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent radio monitoring.
texts_above.3: SP monitored the radio continuously and maintained an accurate picture of every aircraft in the pattern from their reports and the ATC instructions, with clearances read back completely and complied with without delay. The only refinement available was to track the pattern traffic a fraction more continuously still on the busiest circuits. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined radio monitoring.
texts_above.4: SP monitored the radio continuously and maintained an accurate picture of every aircraft in the pattern from their reports and the ATC instructions, including one changed sequence, with radio work integrated into the flying task with no degradation of either. The technique is already sound; nothing in the monitoring needs to change. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary radio monitoring.

error_modes.label: Execution of the pattern per LAP and ATC instructions

texts.0: SP, due to insufficient knowledge of the pattern as published in the LAP, did not execute the traffic pattern according to the LAP and the instructions given by ATC. Legs were flown in the wrong order and a cleared pattern direction was not followed. The IP had to take over the pattern sequence to keep the aircraft in the cleared flow.
texts.1: SP, due to a mental sequence of the pattern that was not fixed before the sortie, did not execute the pattern in accordance with the LAP and the ATC instructions. Two required actions were taken out of sequence and one clearance element was not applied. SP flew the correct sequence only after the IP prompted each step verbally.
texts.2: SP, due to a step of the pattern sequence recalled late, executed one leg out of the order described in the LAP. SP recognized the deviation, restored the published sequence at the next point and applied the ATC instruction correctly from then on. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP executed the traffic pattern according to the LAP and the instructions given by ATC. Every leg, entry and exit was flown in the published sequence and all clearance elements were applied as received. The pattern was completed without prompting or correction.
texts.4: SP executed the traffic pattern exactly as published in the LAP and as instructed by ATC, including an amended sequence issued in flight. Each step was anticipated so the pattern progressed without pause or reconstruction. Actions and radio work were sequenced so that neither delayed the other.
texts.marginal: SP executed the pattern according to the LAP and the ATC instructions, but the sequence was recalled step by step and each leg was set up only after the previous one was complete. Nothing was omitted, yet there was no margin left when the pattern was busy. SP is expected to know the pattern sequence well enough to work one step ahead of the aircraft.

texts_at.0: SP flew the pattern with the IP calling each step of the LAP sequence in turn, since holding the whole sequence in mind rather than recalling it one step at a time has not yet been practiced without that call. texts_at.3: SP held the downwind ground track parallel to the runway at approximately 1/2 mile spacing adjusted for the wind, due to the runway picture being compared to the intended sight picture a fraction after roll-out rather than as part of it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to compare the runway picture to the intended sight picture as part of the roll-out itself.

texts_above.1: SP held the downwind ground track parallel to the runway at approximately 0.45 NM spacing after the drift correction was called doubled. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP held the downwind ground track parallel to the runway on every approach, with drift correction set at approximately twice the correction used on initial and the track staying a comfortable margin inside the 0.5 NM radius from the published pattern points. Offsetting into the wind a moment earlier would widen that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured spacing technique.
texts_above.3: SP derived the downwind drift correction from the correction already flown on initial and offset the ground track into the wind before any drift developed, with spacing staying within a small fraction of the permitted radius. The only refinement available was to offset into the wind a fraction sooner still on the fastest legs. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise spacing technique.
texts_above.4: SP derived the downwind drift correction from the correction already flown on initial and offset the ground track into the wind before any drift developed on every approach, with the perch point falling exactly where it had been planned for the final turn. The technique is already sound; nothing in the drift derivation needs to change. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate spacing technique.

error_modes.label: Perch point arrival on speed, configured and ready for the planned final turn

texts.0: SP, due to power not adjusted to the approximately 30 to 35 percent torque required on downwind and to a configuration completed late, arrived at the perch point slow, out of trim and not ready for the planned 30 degree bank final turn. Airspeed was more than 20 knots below the 120 KIAS minimum and the aircraft was more than 300 feet off pattern altitude at the perch. The IP had to intervene to add power and re-establish the aircraft before the final turn.
texts.1: SP, due to power left where it had been set in the break instead of adjusted to approximately 30 to 35 percent torque, arrived at the perch 20 knots off the planned airspeed, at the limit of the standard, and about 300 feet off pattern altitude. The final turn was entered without a planned bank and the bank had to be changed during the turn. SP added power and set the attitude only after verbal prompting from the IP.
texts.2: SP, due to a perch point identified late against the runway threshold, arrived 12 to 15 knots off the planned airspeed with the aircraft configured but not yet stabilized. SP set approximately 30 to 35 percent torque and re-established pattern altitude within 200 to 250 feet before rolling into a 30 degree bank final turn. The correction was made without IP prompting.
texts.3: SP arrived at the perch point at 120 KIAS minimum, properly configured and trimmed, with power at approximately 30 to 35 percent torque. Airspeed was held within 10 knots and pattern altitude within 150 feet at the roll-in, and the final turn was started at the planned 30 degrees of bank. No adjustment to bank or power was needed during the turn.
texts.4: SP arrived at the perch stabilized within 3 to 5 knots of the planned airspeed and within 30 to 50 feet of pattern altitude, configured and hands off. The perch point had been adjusted for the wind, so the planned 30 degree bank final turn was entered without hesitation and required no bank change. The downwind was completed with time in hand before the roll-in.
texts.marginal: SP reached the perch on parameters, but airspeed and trim settled only at the perch itself and the bank at roll-in had to be judged against the runway rather than flown as a planned value. The standards were met, yet nothing was in reserve if spacing had required a delayed perch. SP is expected to have the aircraft configured, on speed and trimmed well before the perch so that the final turn is entered as planned.

texts_at.0: SP arrived at the perch point with the IP calling for the power to be set for the perch in anticipation of reaching it, since setting that power ahead of the perch rather than once it is identified has not yet been practiced without that call. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to set the power in anticipation independently on the next approach.
texts_at.1: SP arrived at the perch point at 120 KIAS minimum, holding airspeed within approximately 20 knots and pattern altitude within approximately 300 feet at the roll-in, at the outer edge of the standard, due to power being set to approximately 30 to 35 percent torque only once the perch point was already identified rather than in anticipation of it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to set the power for the perch in anticipation of reaching it rather than once it is identified.
texts_at.2: SP arrived at the perch with airspeed within about 15 knots and pattern altitude within about 220 feet, due to the perch point being identified against the runway threshold a beat later than the technique calls for. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to identify the perch point earlier against the runway threshold.
texts_at.3: SP arrived at the perch point at 120 KIAS minimum, properly configured and trimmed, holding airspeed within approximately 10 knots and pattern altitude within approximately 150 feet at the roll-in, due to the final turn bank being confirmed a fraction after roll-in rather than planned before it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to plan the final turn bank before roll-in rather than confirming it during the turn.

texts_above.1: SP arrived at the perch point at 120 KIAS minimum, holding airspeed within approximately 18 knots and pattern altitude within approximately 280 feet at the roll-in after the power setting was called in anticipation. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP arrived at the perch point configured and trimmed on every approach, with power at approximately 30 to 35 percent torque and airspeed within about 12 knots and pattern altitude within about 180 feet at the roll-in. Setting the power for the perch a fraction earlier would tighten both figures further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good perch discipline.
texts_above.3: SP arrived at the perch stabilized within a few knots of the planned airspeed and a few tens of feet of pattern altitude, configured and hands off with the planned bank final turn entered without hesitation on every approach. The only refinement available was to configure a fraction earlier still on the busiest downwinds. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good perch discipline.
texts_above.4: SP arrived at the perch stabilized within a few knots of the planned airspeed and a few tens of feet of pattern altitude on every approach, configured and hands off with the downwind completed with time in hand before the roll-in. The technique is already sound; nothing in the perch sequencing needs to change. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent perch discipline.

error_modes.label: Recognition of abnormal pattern situations and go-around decision

texts.0: SP, due to failure to recognize an abnormal situation developing in the pattern, continued a pattern that no longer matched the published geometry instead of executing a go-around. Deviations grew past 300 feet in altitude and 20 knots in airspeed with the traffic conflict unresolved, and the position of the other aircraft was never queried with the tower. The IP had to direct the go-around and fly the aircraft clear.
texts.1: SP, due to hesitation to abandon a pattern that already looked wrong, delayed the decision to go around. The deviations reached 300 feet and 20 knots, at the limits of the standard, before the aircraft was repositioned, and the tower was queried about the conflicting traffic only after the IP suggested it. The go-around itself was flown correctly once directed.
texts.2: SP, due to abnormal spacing that was assessed but not acted on immediately, allowed the pattern to compress and the deviations to reach 200 to 250 feet and 12 to 15 knots. SP then queried the tower about the position of the preceding aircraft and elected to go around in time, without IP prompting, and the pattern was re-entered normally.
texts.3: SP recognized the abnormal situation in the pattern as it developed and executed a go-around without hesitation, keeping deviations inside 150 feet and 10 knots up to the decision. The tower was queried about the location of the conflicting traffic before the situation could tighten further. The go-around and the pattern re-entry were flown as published.
texts.4: SP identified the developing conflict early from the radio picture and the visual scan and repositioned before any parameter moved appreciably. The decision to go around was made and announced without delay, with deviations of a few knots and a few tens of feet. The pattern was re-entered in sequence with no effect on the other traffic.
texts.marginal: SP executed the go-around and stayed within standards, but the decision came after the situation had been recognized and then reconsidered, and the tower query followed the decision rather than informing it. The outcome was correct, yet the margin between recognizing the problem and acting on it was small. SP is expected to act on the first indication that a pattern or a landing attempt looks or feels wrong rather than to assess whether it can still be salvaged.

texts_at.0: SP flew the pattern with the IP calling the first indication that a go-around was required, since committing to that decision on the first indication rather than a confirming second look has not yet been practiced without that call. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to commit to the decision on the first indication independently on the next pattern.
texts_at.1: SP recognized the abnormal situation in the pattern and executed a go-around, holding the deviations to approximately 280 feet and 20 knots up to the decision, at the outer edge of the standard, due to the decision to go around being confirmed by a second look at the developing spacing rather than made on the first indication. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to commit to the decision on the first indication rather than confirming it with a second look.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the abnormal spacing and elected to go around in time, holding deviations to about 220 feet and 15 knots, due to the query to the tower about the conflicting traffic coming a beat after the decision rather than informing it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to query the tower before the decision is made rather than immediately after it.
texts_at.3: SP recognized the abnormal situation in the pattern as it developed and executed a go-around without hesitation, keeping deviations to approximately 110 feet and 10 knots up to the decision, due to the query to the tower being made a fraction after the situation was first recognized rather than as it was recognized. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to query the tower in the same moment the situation is first recognized.

texts_above.1: SP recognized the abnormal situation in the pattern and executed a go-around, holding the deviations to approximately 280 feet and 18 knots up to the decision after the first indication was called. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the abnormal situation in the pattern as it developed and executed a go-around without hesitation, keeping deviations to about 180 feet and 12 knots up to the decision with the tower queried about the conflicting traffic before the situation could tighten further. Recognizing the trend a moment earlier would narrow both figures further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady go-around judgement.
texts_above.3: SP identified the developing conflict early from the radio picture and the visual scan and repositioned before any parameter moved appreciably, with the decision to go around made and announced without delay. The only refinement available was to reposition a fraction earlier still on the tightest sequences. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed go-around judgement.
texts_above.4: SP identified the developing conflict early from the radio picture and the visual scan and repositioned before any parameter moved appreciably on every occasion, with deviations of only a few knots and a few tens of feet and the pattern re-entered in sequence with no effect on the other traffic. The technique is already sound; nothing in the recognition needs to change. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional go-around judgement.

error_modes.label: Break to downwind combined: altitude gained in the break and the airspeed still high at the perch

texts.0: SP, due to the back pressure in the break being held with the power left at the initial setting, let the aircraft climb more than 300 ft above pattern altitude through the break and arrive on downwind more than 20 kt fast. The gear was selected with the airspeed above the limit, with the result that a limitation was exceeded and the perch was reached unconfigured. The IP took the controls and flew the go-around.
texts.1: SP, due to the power reduction in the break being made after the bank was on rather than with it, gained 300 ft in the break, at the limit of the tolerance, and arrived at the perch 20 kt fast, at the limit, with the result that the configuration was completed late on downwind. SP reduced the power only after the IP called the airspeed. The gear was selected within the limitation.
texts.2: SP, due to the back pressure in the break being a fraction more than the level turn required, gained about 200 ft above pattern altitude in the break and arrived at the perch about 15 kt fast, between the desired and the maximum tolerance on both, with the result that the configuration and the descent to pattern altitude were made together on downwind. SP recognized the altitude and the airspeed, reduced the power and regained pattern altitude before the perch without prompting. The gear was selected within the limitation.
texts.3: SP flew the break as a level turn with the power reduced as the bank went on, stayed within 150 ft of pattern altitude and arrived at the perch within 10 kt of the target, configured in sequence on downwind. No prompting was required.
texts.4: SP flew the break with the bank, the back pressure and the power reduction as one movement, the altitude within a few feet of pattern altitude and the airspeed within a few knots at the perch every time. Nothing in the break needed a correction.
texts.marginal: SP kept the break inside the required standard, but the altitude sat near the 150 ft high edge of the band on most breaks and the airspeed near the 10 kt fast edge at the perch, the power reduced a beat after the bank each time. The tendency is to hold the back pressure past the level turn. SP is expected to reduce the power as the bank goes on in the break.

texts_at.0: SP flew the break with the IP calling the power reduction, the bank and the level turn, since flying the break as a level decelerating turn has not yet been practiced. The aircraft climbed well above pattern altitude and arrived on downwind well fast because the power was left at the initial setting. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to reduce the power with the bank on the next break.
texts_at.1: SP gained about 300 ft in the break and arrived at the perch about 20 kt fast, at the outer edge of the standard on both, due to the power reduction being made after the bank was on rather than with it. The power was reduced after the IP called the airspeed. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to reduce the power as the bank goes on.
texts_at.2: SP gained about 200 ft above pattern altitude in the break and arrived at the perch about 15 kt fast, due to the back pressure being a fraction more than the level turn required. SP recognized the altitude and the airspeed and regained pattern altitude before the perch without prompting. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to fly the break as a level turn.
texts_at.3: SP stayed within about 150 ft of pattern altitude in the break and arrived at the perch within 10 kt of the target, due to the power reduction being a fraction smaller than the deceleration to downwind required. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to size the power reduction to the deceleration required.

texts_above.1: SP regained pattern altitude and the downwind airspeed from about 300 ft high and about 20 kt fast at the perch, at the tolerance limit on both, configuring within the limitation. The power reduction followed a verbal call from the IP on the airspeed. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the aircraft about 200 ft above pattern altitude after the break and about 15 kt fast at the perch, reduced the power and regained pattern altitude before the perch without prompting, configuring within the limitation. Flying the break as a level turn with the power reduced as the bank goes on would keep both on the targets. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound break technique.
texts_above.3: SP flew every break as a level turn with the power reduced as the bank went on, stayed within 120 ft of pattern altitude and arrived at the perch within 8 kt of the target. The only refinement available was to size the power reduction to the deceleration a little more closely. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise break technique.
texts_above.4: SP flew every break with the bank, the back pressure and the power reduction as one movement, the altitude within a few feet of pattern altitude and the airspeed within a few knots at the perch. The technique is already sound; nothing in the break needs to change. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional break technique.

error_modes.label: Downwind to final: roll-out heading off and the altitude off together after a rushed final turn
error_modes.source: specific:EXIT HEADING (degrees)|specific:ALTITUDE (feet)|technique:5.8 PERCH AND FINAL TURN

texts.0: SP, due to the final turn being started from the perch with the bank rolled on before the power was reduced and the nose lowered, flew the turn tight and high and rolled out more than 10 degrees through the final heading, more than 300 ft above the normal final altitude. The overshoot was corrected with a steep bank at low airspeed, with the result that the final could not be stabilized. The IP called the go-around.
texts.1: SP, due to the sequence of power, nose and bank at the perch being compressed into one movement, rolled out 10 degrees off the final heading, at the limit of the tolerance, and 300 ft above the normal final altitude, at the limit, with the result that the final was stabilized only on short final. SP corrected the heading and the glide path only after the IP called them. The landing was made within the tolerance.
texts.2: SP, due to the bank in the final turn being rolled on a beat before the nose was lowered, rolled out about 8 degrees off the final heading and about 200 ft above the normal final altitude, between the desired and the maximum tolerance on both, with the result that a correction was needed early on final. SP recognized the heading against the runway and the height against the aim point, corrected both and stabilized the final without prompting. The landing was made as planned.
texts.3: SP started the final turn from the perch with the power, the nose and the bank in sequence, rolled out within 5 degrees of the final heading and 150 ft of the normal final altitude on the extended centerline. No prompting was required.
texts.4: SP flew every final turn from the perch with the power, the nose and the bank in an unhurried sequence and rolled out on the final heading within a degree or two, within a few feet of the normal final altitude. Nothing in the final turn needed a correction.
texts.marginal: SP kept the final turn inside the required standard, but the roll-out sat near the 5 degree edge of the heading band and near the 150 ft high edge of the altitude band on most patterns, the turn started with the bank ahead of the nose. The tendency is to rush the sequence at the perch. SP is expected to start the final turn with the power and the nose before the bank.

texts_at.0: SP flew the final turn with the IP calling the power, the nose and the bank at the perch and the roll-out point, since the sequence at the perch and the roll-out on the extended centerline have not yet been practiced. The roll-out was well through the final heading and high because the turn was flown tight. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to lower the nose before the bank at the perch on the next pattern.
texts_at.1: SP rolled out about 10 degrees off the final heading and about 300 ft above the normal final altitude, at the outer edge of the standard on both, due to the sequence at the perch being compressed into one movement. The heading and the glide path were corrected after the IP called them. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to fly the sequence at the perch in order.
texts_at.2: SP rolled out about 8 degrees off the final heading and about 200 ft above the normal final altitude, due to the bank being rolled on a beat before the nose was lowered. SP recognized both against the runway and the aim point and corrected without prompting. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to lower the nose before the bank at the perch.
texts_at.3: SP rolled out within about 5 degrees of the final heading and 150 ft of the normal final altitude, due to the roll-out being started a fraction late for the bank in use. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to lead the roll-out for the bank in use.

texts_above.1: SP stabilized the final from about 10 degrees off the final heading and about 300 ft above the normal final altitude, at the tolerance limit on both, and landed within the tolerance. The corrections followed a verbal call from the IP on the heading and the glide path. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the roll-out about 8 degrees off the final heading and about 200 ft above the normal final altitude against the runway and the aim point, corrected both and stabilized the final without prompting. Lowering the nose before the bank at the perch would put the roll-out on the heading and the altitude. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to steady final turn technique.
texts_above.3: SP started every final turn from the perch with the power, the nose and the bank in sequence and rolled out within 4 degrees of the final heading and 120 ft of the normal final altitude on the extended centerline. The only refinement available was to lead the roll-out for the bank in use a fraction earlier. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to well-developed final turn technique.
texts_above.4: SP flew every final turn from the perch with the power, the nose and the bank in an unhurried sequence and rolled out on the final heading within a degree or two, within a few feet of the normal final altitude. The technique is already sound; nothing in the final turn needs to change. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to superior final turn technique.

error_modes.label: Final turn planning with the wind: perch point and bank adjusted for the crosswind, roll-out short of or through the extended centerline
error_modes.source: technique:5.8 PERCH AND FINAL TURN|technique:5.9 FINAL

texts.0: SP, due to retention of the no-wind perch picture after the tower had reported a strong crosswind blowing the downwind toward the runway, started the final turn at the standard perch with the standard bank. The turn was blown through the extended centerline by more than 10 degrees and the correction was made with a steep bank at low airspeed inside the normal final altitude, with the result that the final could not be stabilized. The IP called the go-around.
texts.1: SP, due to an incomplete mental model of the wind effect on the final turn, adjusted the perch for the wind but flew the turn with the standard bank, with the result that the aircraft rolled out 10 degrees through the extended centerline, at the limit of the tolerance, and 300 ft above the normal final altitude. SP corrected back to the centerline only after the IP called the overshoot. The final was stabilized on short final.
texts.2: SP, due to a wind correction in the final turn a little smaller than the crosswind required, rolled out about 8 degrees through the extended centerline and about 200 ft above the normal final altitude, between the desired and the maximum tolerance on both, with the result that a correction back to the centerline was needed early on final. SP recognized the overshoot against the runway, corrected it and stabilized the final without prompting. The landing was made as planned.
texts.3: SP planned the final turn for the reported wind, displacing the perch and adjusting the bank so the roll-out fell on the extended centerline within 5 degrees of the final heading and 150 ft of the normal final altitude. No prompting was required.
texts.4: SP built the wind into every final turn before the perch, displacing the perch and sizing the bank so the roll-out fell on the extended centerline within a degree or two and a few feet of the normal final altitude. Nothing in the wind planning needed a correction.
texts.marginal: SP kept the final turn inside the required standard with the wind, but the roll-out sat near the 5 degree edge of the band on the downwind side on most patterns, the wind allowed for in the bank a beat late each time. The tendency is to under-correct the final turn for the crosswind. SP is expected to plan the perch and the bank for the full reported wind.

texts_at.0: SP flew the final turn in a crosswind with the IP calling the displaced perch, the bank and the roll-out, since planning the final turn for the wind has not yet been practiced. The aircraft rolled out well through the extended centerline because the no-wind perch and bank were flown. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to displace the perch for the reported wind on the next pattern.
texts_at.1: SP rolled out about 10 degrees through the extended centerline and about 300 ft above the normal final altitude, at the outer edge of the standard on both, due to the bank in the turn being left at the standard value while the perch was adjusted. The correction back to the centerline followed the IP call. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to adjust the bank with the perch for the wind.
texts_at.2: SP rolled out about 8 degrees through the extended centerline and about 200 ft above the normal final altitude, due to a wind correction in the final turn a little smaller than the crosswind required. SP recognized the overshoot against the runway and corrected without prompting. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to size the wind correction to the reported crosswind.
texts_at.3: SP rolled out within about 5 degrees of the final heading and 150 ft of the normal final altitude with the wind, due to the perch being displaced a fraction less than the reported crosswind called for. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to displace the perch for the full reported wind.

texts_above.1: SP stabilized the final from about 10 degrees through the extended centerline and about 300 ft above the normal final altitude, at the tolerance limit on both, in the crosswind. The correction back to the centerline followed a verbal call from the IP on the overshoot. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the roll-out about 8 degrees through the extended centerline and about 200 ft above the normal final altitude against the runway, corrected it and stabilized the final without prompting in the crosswind. Sizing the wind correction to the reported crosswind would put the roll-out on the centerline. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to dependable wind planning in the final turn.
texts_above.3: SP planned every final turn for the reported wind, displacing the perch and adjusting the bank so the roll-out fell on the extended centerline within 4 degrees of the final heading and 120 ft of the normal final altitude. The only refinement available was to displace the perch for the full reported wind. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to consistently accurate wind planning in the final turn.
texts_above.4: SP built the wind into every final turn before the perch, displacing the perch and sizing the bank so the roll-out fell on the extended centerline within a degree or two and a few feet of the normal final altitude. The technique is already sound; nothing in the wind planning needs to change. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to faultless wind planning in the final turn.
